audit_metadata.gateway: theteller.net (real HTTP, dev fallback to synthetic checkout)

summary.current_architecture: Next.js 16 App Router route handlers + Prisma ORM + SQLite (default), with an in-memory rate limiter, inline webhook dispatcher, and synchronous Prisma $transaction blocks as the only concurrency primitive. Docker-compose declares Postgres + Redis but the app code uses SQLite unless DATABASE_URL is overridden. There is no background worker, no durable queue, no saga orchestration, and no scheduled-job processor.
current_architecture_limitations_for_fin: SQLite serialises all writes through a single WAL — concurrent payments, payouts, and webhook deliveries stall under any real write load.

No durable execution: a process restart mid-payment loses in-flight state. The /callback route re-asks the gateway, but only because TheTeller is stateful; internal multi-step flows (payroll, payouts) have no resumption.
No saga pattern: a payout that debits ledger but fails at the rail has no automatic compensation. Code is 'create pending row + hope'.
No retry policy beyond the webhook dispatcher's inline setTimeout loop — which itself dies with the process.

No idempotency locking: the idempotency check is a TOCTOU read-then-write. Two identical POSTs race past the read, both create the resource, and the second insert is silently swallowed (P2002 catch). Double-charge / double-payout is possible.
In-memory rate limiter is per-process — instant 2x–Nx the limit by spinning up N replicas.
No tenant isolation: every API key resolves to the same demo Customer via getOrCreateDemoCustomer().
No callback signature verification on /payments/callback — anyone who learns a payment reference can drive the state machine.
No background workers: /payroll/runs creates 'scheduled' rows that never execute.
Audit logs are fire-and-forget — compliance records are silently dropped on transient DB errors.
No structured logging, no trace propagation — the middleware generates x-request-id but routes never include it in console.error output.

golang_plus_temporal.verdict: RECOMMENDED — correct choice for the payment-orchestration core.
why: Temporal solves exactly the problems Nexora has: durable workflows, automatic retry with backoff, saga compensation, long-running transactions, human-in-the-loop, and code-level versioning of workflows (Patch + Versioning APIs).

A payment is naturally a workflow: Authorise → Capture → Settle → Notify → (Refund on failure). Each activity is idempotent, retryable, and compensatable. Temporal models this directly with `workflow.ExecuteActivity` + retry Policy + compensation activities.
Go's concurrency (goroutines, channels), small binary, ~10ms cold start, and strong HTTP/gRPC story are ideal for the high-throughput gateway tier in front of Temporal.
Temporal is production-proven at Snap, Stripe, Coinbase, Datadog, and HashiCorp for exactly this use case.
Temporal's deterministic-replay model means a process crash mid-workflow is invisible to the user — the workflow resumes from the last completed activity on a different worker.

Migration path is the cleanest of any alternative: Temporal workflows are invoked over gRPC; the Next.js route handler can call `StartWorkflow` and poll for the result, so the strangler fig is mechanical.
caveats: Temporal is infrastructure, not a library: you run a Temporal Server cluster (or use Temporal Cloud). For a startup, start on Temporal Cloud (~$0.04/workflow-execution) and self-host later.
Go has a smaller West-African talent pool than Node.js. Mitigation: keep Next.js/TS for the dashboard/BFF, hire 1–2 senior Go engineers for the orchestration core.
Workflow determinism is a discipline: don't call `time.Now()` or `Math.random()` inside workflow code — use Temporal's `workflow.Now()` and `workflow.SideEffect()`.

rust_plus_tokio.verdict: NOT RECOMMENDED for the orchestration tier.
why: Max performance and memory safety are real strengths — relevant for a low-latency matching engine or HFT, not for a payment gateway whose bottleneck is the upstream gateway and DB.
No Temporal-quality durable-workflow engine in Rust. You would build saga/compensation/replay from scratch (or use `actix`/`axum` + hand-rolled state machines). That is 6+ months of hard engineering.
Iteration speed is 2–3x slower than Go; the talent pool is 5–10x smaller in Lagos/Accra/Nairobi.
Overkill: Nexora's QPS is bounded by gateway round-trips (~50–500ms each), not by CPU. Go + Temporal already handles millions of workflows per worker.
rust_plus_tokio.where_it_would_fit: Only for a future hot path — e.g. an internal FX-routing engine or a card-authorisation switch where microseconds matter.

elixir_plus_phoenix.verdict: VIABLE alternative, but with higher team risk.
why: BEAM VM is exceptional for fault-tolerant, concurrent, soft-realtime systems — Discord and WhatsApp run on it for good reason. Supervision trees + hot code reload are genuinely superior to anything in Go for long-running processes.

Oban (Postgres-backed) + Broadway (Kafka/Redis consumer) are excellent durable-job libraries — but they are not a workflow engine. You would still hand-roll saga/compensation/versioning, which is what Temporal gives you for free.
Smaller ecosystem for African payment rails (Paystack, Flutterwave, TheTeller SDKs are JS/Go first). Smaller hiring pool than Go.
Best fit if the team already knows Elixir; otherwise the 3-month ramp-up is hard to justify.

nodejs_plus_bullmq.verdict: Tempting (stay in TS) but underpowered for orchestration.
why: BullMQ is a great Redis-backed job queue — for fire-and-forget jobs (webhook delivery, email, KYC async). It is NOT a workflow engine: no saga pattern, no deterministic replay, no compensation, no human-in-the-loop, no workflow versioning.
You would build those primitives yourself. By the time you've built a workflow engine on BullMQ, you've reinvented a worse Temporal.

Stay in TS for the dashboard/BFF, but don't try to solve durable orchestration with BullMQ alone. (BullMQ + a hand-rolled saga is fine for the simpler flows — payouts, payroll — but not for the core payment flow.)
nodejs_plus_bullmq.where_it_fits: Use BullMQ for the webhook dispatcher and KYC async verification — both of which are currently broken (inline setTimeout / stubbed).

java_plus_spring_cloud.verdict: Enterprise-grade but heavyweight for a startup.
why: Spring Cloud Stream + Kafka + Spring Cloud Saga can do everything Temporal does, with mature tooling and a huge talent pool.
Cost: JVM warmup (200–500ms), ~512MB+ RSS per service, verbose XML/annotation config, slower iteration than Go. Spring Cloud Saga is also more code than Temporal for the same workflow.
Justified if you're an enterprise with existing Spring investment; not justified for a 5–15-engineer fintech startup choosing greenfield.
Hiring is easy (lots of Java engineers in Africa), but the culture fit with a Next.js front-end shop is poor.

issues.title: Idempotency-Key TOCTOU race is NOT fixed — duplicate charges/payouts possible
issues.description: checkIdempotency reads the IdempotencyRecord row, returns null if not found, and the handler then does the work (creates Payment row, calls TheTeller gateway, dispatches webhook, then saveIdempotencyRecord inserts the row). Two concurrent requests with the same Idempotency-Key both pass the read (both see 'not found'), both create a Payment, both call the gateway, and the second saveIdempotencyRecord hits P2002 which is silently caught with a `// race — safe to ignore` comment. By then the double-charge has already happened. This is the classic Time-Of-Check-Time-Of-Use race; the catch only papers over the symptom, not the cause.
issues.fix: Use a Postgres advisory lock keyed on the idempotency-key hash (pg_advisory_xact_lock) inside a transaction, OR insert the IdempotencyRecord FIRST with `INSERT … ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING` and only proceed if the insert returned a row. The current read-then-write pattern is broken. Switch to Postgres to get row-level locks; SQLite's serialised writes happen to mask this in dev but won't in prod.

issues.title: SQLite is the default database — unsuitable for fintech OLTP
issues.description: schema.prisma declares `provider = "sqlite"` and env.example ships `DATABASE_URL=file:…/custom.db`. SQLite serialises all writes through a single WAL writer, has no row-level locking, no native JSON (used by auditLog metadata and webhook payloads), no LISTEN/NOTIFY, and a 1GB-ish practical working-set ceiling. Concurrent payments + payouts + webhook deliveries will stall under any real load. Docker-compose already declares a Postgres 16 service but the app code never uses it unless DATABASE_URL is manually overridden AND `prisma db push` is re-run with `provider = "postgresql"`.
issues.fix: Switch `provider = "postgresql"` in schema.prisma, run `prisma migrate dev` against the docker-compose Postgres, add `@db.Text`/JSONB annotations for the String-typed JSON columns (metadata, payload, responseBody), add proper indexes for the new query patterns (see issue on missing indexes), and require DATABASE_URL to be a `postgresql://` URL in production via a startup assertion.

issues.title: Webhook dispatcher uses inline setTimeout backoff — dies with the process
issues.description: deliverWithBackoff loops up to 5 attempts with `await delay(BACKOFF_SECONDS[attempt-1] * 1000)` — that's 1m + 5m + 30m + 2h + 6h = up to 8h41m of in-process sleep. dispatchWebhook fires this with `.catch()` (fire-and-forget), but the promise only lives as long as the Node process. On serverless (Vercel) the request lifecycle is <10s and the function is frozen after the response is sent; on a long-lived Node server a restart, deploy, or crash kills every in-flight retry. The code comment admits this: 'in production this would be a delayed queue, not an in-process sleep'. For a fintech, losing a `payment.succeeded` webhook means a merchant never ships the order.
issues.fix: Replace with a durable queue. Two viable paths: (a) BullMQ on Redis with delayed jobs (cheap, TS-native, sufficient for Nexora's volume), or (b) a Temporal workflow `DeliverWebhookWorkflow` with retry policy and `workflow.Sleep()` between attempts (gives replay safety + visibility). Either way, the dispatcher should only enqueue the job and update WebhookEvent.nextAttemptAt; the actual HTTP POST happens in the worker. Add `delivered=false, nextAttemptAt<now`-based drain queries.

issues.title: Rate limiting is in-memory only — instant bypass via horizontal scaling
issues.description: Rate-limit state is a `Map<string, Bucket>` per Node process. Run 4 replicas behind a load balancer and an attacker gets 4× the limit (or Nx for N replicas). The middleware comment admits it: 'For multi-instance deploys, back this with Upstash Redis'. For a fintech with a public API this is an abuse / DoS vector — a single attacker can mint noise at 4×30 = 120 req/min anonymous, or 4×1000 = 4000 req/min with a $0-cost fake `nxp_live_…` key (see issue on permissive getApiKeyMode).
issues.fix: Use Upstash Redis REST (@upstash/ratelimit) — already wired in env.example (UPSTASH_REDIS_REST_URL/TOKEN). For self-hosted, use a Redis-backed token bucket (ioredis + Lua script for atomic check-and-decrement). Slide the rate-limit logic out of edge middleware and into a server-side helper if you need sub-millisecond latency, or accept the 5–10ms cost of Redis per request.

issues.title: No callback signature verification on /payments/callback
issues.description: TheTeller redirects the customer back to /api/v1/payments/callback?transaction_id=… after checkout. The route accepts this with no HMAC verification — anyone who learns a payment's reference (which is returned in the POST /v1/payments response) can hit the callback URL. In production the route calls verifyTransaction() on the gateway first, so the attacker can't force a 'succeeded' status without a real succeeded transaction at TheTeller — but they can still drive the state machine and trigger webhook fanout. In dev mode (`NODE_ENV !== 'production'`) the route has a fallback that FORCES status to 'succeeded' when verification fails (line 81–85), so any unauthenticated call to the callback with a valid reference completes the payment.
issues.fix: Verify TheTeller's signature on the redirect (they support HMAC-signed callbacks; see their docs). Reject if the signature is missing or invalid. Remove the dev-mode force-succeeded fallback entirely — gate it behind an explicit `THETELLER_ALLOW_UNVERIFIED_CALLBACKS=1` flag instead of `NODE_ENV !== 'production'`, so staging environments don't auto-succeed payments. Always require signature verification in prod.

issues.title: Hardcoded fallback sandbox API key in source code
issues.description: GET /api/v1/sandbox-key returns `process.env.NEXORA_SANDBOX_KEY || 'nxp_test_8h2k9nbq01def456abc789'`. The fallback key is committed to source, shipped in the bundle, seeded into every dev DB by scripts/seed.ts, and valid on any deployed instance that ran the seed. The route is unauthenticated and returns the key to anyone — verified live: `curl /api/v1/sandbox-key` returns `{data:{key:'nxp_test_8h2k9nbq01def456abc789',mode:'test'}}`. The route comment claims the key is 'safe to ship in the client bundle' — it is not: it's a real key that creates real payments, payouts, virtual cards, and foreign accounts on the demo DB.
issues.fix: Remove the hardcoded fallback. Require NEXORA_SANDBOX_KEY in all environments (fail with 503 if unset). For the public endpoint explorer, issue a per-session ephemeral test key from a separate /v1/sandbox-key/issue endpoint with a 1h TTL, instead of one shared key.

issues.title: Master key is bypassed in every non-prod environment
issues.description: requireMasterKey returns `null` (allow) when NEXORA_MASTER_KEY is unset and `NODE_ENV !== 'production'`. This is correct for localhost but catastrophic for a staging/preview environment that's internet-reachable: anyone can POST to /v1/api-keys with no x-master-key header and mint live API keys. Vercel preview deployments, Render PR environments, and any Docker image run with NODE_ENV=development are wide open.
issues.fix: Require NEXORA_MASTER_KEY in every environment except `localhost`/`127.0.0.1`. Check `req.nextUrl.hostname` or process.env.HOST, not just NODE_ENV. Or: always require the master key, and provide a `npm run dev` setup script that generates and injects a random one into .env.local.

issues.title: No background workers — payroll runs never execute, scheduled jobs never run
issues.description: POST /v1/payroll/runs creates a PayrollRun row with status='scheduled' and a scheduledFor timestamp — and that's it. There is no worker, no cron, no queue consumer that ever picks up scheduled runs and marks them paid. The endpoint is a write-only TODO. Same for any other scheduled job (e.g. expiring payment links, retrying failed payouts, garbage-collecting expired idempotency records beyond the opportunistic read-time delete). The 'payroll' feature is non-functional in production.
issues.fix: Add a worker process. Cheapest: a BullMQ scheduler that polls PayrollRun where scheduledFor<now AND status='scheduled' every minute and enqueues a ProcessPayrollRunJob. Correct: a Temporal workflow `PayrollRunWorkflow` started from POST /v1/payroll/runs with `workflow.ExecuteTimer` until scheduledFor, then fan-out to per-employee PayoutWorkflows. Either way, this requires a separate `worker` process in the deploy (add to docker-compose, Procfile, or Vercel's cron + external worker).

issues.title: Demo customer is shared across all API keys — multi-tenant data leak
issues.description: getOrCreateDemoCustomer() always returns the same Customer (`john.doe@nexora.africa`). POST /v1/payments, /v1/virtual-cards, /v1/foreign-accounts, /v1/kyc/verify-bvn all resolve the customer through this helper unless a customerId is explicitly passed — and even then the API key's userId is the scoping primitive, not the customer's. Two merchants with different live API keys both create payments on the same demo Customer row, see the same KYC status, and would see each other's customer-level data on any customer-scoped query. In production this leaks PII across tenants.
issues.fix: Resolve the Customer from the API key's userId via Customer.userId (already indexed). Drop getOrCreateDemoCustomer entirely. Require a customerId on POST /v1/payments (reject if missing or if it doesn't belong to key.userId). For the dashboard demo, create one demo Customer per seeded API key.

issues.title: Missing CRUD: no GET (list) on /v1/payments
issues.description: POST /v1/payments exists but GET /v1/payments does not — you can create payments and fetch one by id, but you cannot list them. This is inconsistent with /v1/payouts, /v1/transactions, /v1/virtual-cards, /v1/foreign-accounts, and /v1/payroll/runs, all of which implement GET-list with the same pagination shape. Merchants building dashboards cannot render a payment history without paginating through all of their payment IDs out-of-band.
issues.fix: Add `export async function GET(req)` to /v1/payments/route.ts that mirrors the /v1/payouts GET handler: authenticate, parse limit/offset via listTransactionsSchema, scope to key.userId, optionally filter by status/reference/currency, return the same `{object:'list', has_more, url, data:[…]}` envelope. Add a `@@index([userId, createdAt])` (already present) — verify it's used.

issues.title: Missing CRUD: no refunds — no PATCH/POST /v1/payments/[id]/refund
issues.description: The Payment model has status `pending | succeeded | failed` and no `refunded` / `partially_refunded` state. There is no PATCH /v1/payments/[id] and no POST /v1/payments/[id]/refund endpoint. A fintech cannot ship without refunds — full stop. The TheTeller integration also has no refund call (only initiatePayment + verifyTransaction). Merchants who need to refund have no API surface.
issues.fix: Add `refunded` and `partially_refunded` to Payment.status, add a Refund model (id, paymentId, amount, reason, status, gatewayRefundId, createdAt), add POST /v1/payments/[id]/refunds, extend the TheTeller gateway module with `initiateRefund()`, and run the whole flow as a Temporal workflow so a partial refund that fails mid-way can be compensated.

issues.title: Missing CRUD: no DELETE/PATCH on virtual-cards/[id], foreign-accounts/[id], webhooks/endpoints/[id]
issues.description: Virtual cards have a PATCH (freeze/unfreeze) but no DELETE (the model has a 'deleted' status that can only be set via direct DB update — there's no endpoint). Foreign accounts have GET only — no PATCH (status, label) and no DELETE (close account). Webhook endpoints have POST + GET-list but no GET/[id], no PATCH (toggle enabled, edit event_types), no DELETE — once registered, an endpoint lives forever. The CRUD surface is asymmetric across resources.
issues.fix: Add PATCH /v1/virtual-cards/[id] with body `{status:'deleted'}` (soft delete, keep row for ledger), or DELETE that sets status='deleted' and zeros the spending limit. Add PATCH + DELETE on /v1/foreign-accounts/[id] (status='closed' on delete). Add /v1/webhooks/endpoints/[id] route.ts with GET, PATCH (enabled, event_types, url), and DELETE. Each PATCH/DELETE should write an audit log entry.

issues.title: PaymentLink route persists nothing — no model, no retrieval, no PATCH/DELETE
issues.description: POST /v1/payment-links generates a `plink_<id>` and `nxp-<slug>` on the fly, returns a `https://pay.nexora.africa/l/<slug>` URL, and persists NOTHING — the code comment says 'no PaymentLink model in schema — for demo we generate the URL on the fly'. There is no GET /v1/payment-links, no GET /v1/payment-links/[id], no PATCH, no DELETE, and no way to look up a link after it's created. The link is dead on creation. The slug collides with itself across requests because nothing dedupes.
issues.fix: Add a PaymentLink model (id, slug @unique, amount, currency, title, description, redirectUrl, status, userId, expiresAt, createdAt). Persist on POST. Add GET (list), GET /[id], PATCH (status: active|expired|disabled), DELETE. The slug should be checked for uniqueness before insert; on conflict, regenerate.

issues.title: Missing CRUD: no PATCH/DELETE/execute on /v1/payroll/runs/[id]
issues.description: Payroll runs can be created (POST) and retrieved (GET), but cannot be cancelled (no PATCH to set status='cancelled' before scheduledFor), cannot be executed on demand (no POST /v1/payroll/runs/[id]/execute), and cannot be deleted. Combined with the missing background worker (see other issue), a scheduled payroll run sits forever in 'scheduled' state with no way for the merchant to cancel it.
issues.fix: Add PATCH /v1/payroll/runs/[id] with body `{status:'cancelled'}` (only valid while status='scheduled'). Add POST /v1/payroll/runs/[id]/execute that starts a Temporal PayrollRunWorkflow immediately (or use the scheduledFor time as a workflow timer). Document the state machine: scheduled → running → paid|failed|cancelled.

issues.title: KYC vendor integration is a stub — verifyBvnViaVendor always returns true
issues.description: verifyBvnViaVendor() is a one-line stub: `return { verified: true }`. The route only invokes it when `KYC_LIVE=1` AND `NODE_ENV=production`, so in dev every BVN verifies — which is fine for the demo. But the stub is also what runs in production if KYC_LIVE is set without a real vendor integration. The code comment is a TODO; there is no env check that fails loud if KYC_LIVE=1 but no YOUVERIFY_API_KEY / SMILE_IDENTITY_* is set. Sanctions/PEP screening is also defaulted to 'unknown' and never run.
issues.fix: Implement the real vendor call (Youverify or Smile Identity). Add a startup assertion: if KYC_LIVE=1, require at least one vendor's API key. On verification, run sanctions (OFAC/UN/EU/HMT) and PEP screening via the same vendor or a dedicated screening API (e.g. ComplyAdvantage). Store the vendor verification reference in AuditLog.metadata. Set kycTier based on the verification depth (tier 1 = BVN only, tier 2 = BVN + ID, tier 3 = BVN + ID + address proof).

issues.title: Audit logs are fire-and-forget — compliance records silently dropped
issues.description: auditLog() calls `db.auditLog.create(...).catch(e => console.error(...))` — fire-and-forget. For a fintech this is a compliance violation: audit logs are required by CBN/SEC/FCA regulators and must be durable. If the DB has a transient error, the audit entry is gone (only in stdout, which is also unstructured). The function also doesn't propagate the request_id from the middleware, so audit entries can't be correlated with the request trace.
issues.fix: Write audit logs synchronously inside the same Prisma transaction as the state change (so they commit atomically). For high-volume endpoints where that's too slow, write to a durable queue (Kafka/Redis Stream) and have a worker persist them with at-least-once semantics and a dead-letter queue. Always include the request_id, the API key id, and a structured before/after diff in metadata. Use JSONB for metadata in Postgres.

issues.title: No request body size limit — memory DoS via large bodies
issues.description: parseBody() does `await req.text()` with no size check, then `JSON.parse(text)`. A 100MB body is read into a JS string and parsed. An attacker with a valid (or fake) API key can OOM the process with a single 1GB POST. Next.js's body parser has a default limit but route handlers using `req.text()` bypass it.
issues.fix: Check `req.headers.get('content-length')` and reject >256KB (or 1MB for file upload routes) with 413 before reading the body. Or read the body as a stream and abort if it exceeds the limit. Use `zod`'s `z.string().max(N)` after parsing for a second layer of defense.

issues.title: Foreign-account number uses Math.random() — predictable and collision-prone
issues.description: The USD/GBP/CNY account number is `String(Math.floor(1_000_000_000 + Math.random() * 8_999_999_999))`. Math.random() is not cryptographically secure and has a ~2^52 period — predictable and collision-prone. Two concurrent requests can also generate the same number (no uniqueness check). The EUR branch uses randomId (crypto.randomBytes) which is correct, but the others don't. There's also no checksum (IBAN mod-97) so a typo'd account number silently routes to the wrong account.
issues.fix: Use crypto.randomBytes for all branches. For EUR, generate a real IBAN with mod-97 checksum. For USD, validate against ABA routing checksum. Add a `@unique` constraint on (userId, accountNumber, currency) and retry on P2002 with a fresh number. Persist the number through a Temporal workflow so a partner-bank API can issue the real number asynchronously.

issues.title: Permissive getApiKeyMode in middleware — fake live keys get 1000 req/min
issues.description: getApiKeyMode() only regex-matches the key format (`nxp_(test|live)_[a-z0-9]+`), it doesn't validate against the DB. So a fake key like `nxp_live_aaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaa` gets the live rate limit (1000/min) without ever hitting the authenticate() DB lookup. An attacker can mint rate-limit headroom for free and crowd out legitimate live keys. The rate-limit key is also `key:${mode}:${ip}` — so the attacker just needs to rotate IPs to multiply the limit further.
issues.fix: Rate-limit by IP for unauthenticated/invalid keys (low limit, e.g. 30/min). Only grant the elevated per-key limit after authenticate() succeeds. Move the rate-limit check to AFTER authentication in the route handler, or do a cheap Redis lookup in middleware to confirm the key exists. Use `key:${keyHash}` (not `key:${mode}:${ip}`) as the rate-limit key so the limit is per-key, not per-IP-per-mode.

issues.title: 405 responses to GET on POST-only routes omit the Allow header (RFC 7231 violation)
issues.description: Verified live: `curl -i -X GET /v1/payments` returns `HTTP/1.1 405 Method Not Allowed` with NO `Allow` header in the response. RFC 7231 §6.5.5 requires a 405 to include an `Allow` header listing the allowed methods. Next.js only sets `Allow` on the OPTIONS preflight response (verified: OPTIONS returns `allow: OPTIONS, POST`), not on the 405 from a missing method export. The body is also empty — clients get no JSON error envelope, unlike every other error response in the API.
issues.fix: Add an explicit method guard at the top of each POST-only route handler (or in a shared helper) that returns `errorResponse('Method not allowed', 405, 'method_not_allowed')` with `headers: { Allow: 'POST' }`. Or add a catch-all route handler that does this for any method not exported. Stripe's API returns a structured 405 with Allow — match that contract.

issues.title: No structured logging — console.error only, no request_id correlation
issues.description: All error logging is `console.error('Payment creation failed:', e?.code || e?.message)`. The middleware generates an `x-request-id` and sets it on the response, but no route handler reads it or includes it in logs. There's no log level (info/warn/error), no JSON structure, no timestamp, no actor (apiKeyId, userId), and no trace context. In production with 100s of concurrent requests, a single `console.error` line is unattributable. Sentry DSN is in env.example but never imported or initialised.
issues.fix: Use pino (or next-logger) with a per-request child logger bound to the request_id, apiKeyId, userId, and route. Log JSON to stdout. Initialise Sentry at app startup (`Sentry.init`) and capture unhandled exceptions. Add a `request_id` to every audit log entry. For the orchestration tier (Go service), use Zap or zerolog with the same trace ID propagated via gRPC metadata.

issues.title: TheTeller amount encoding is fragile for non-2-decimal currencies
issues.description: Amount is encoded as `String(Math.round(args.amount * 100)).padStart(12, '0')` — assumes 2 decimal places. This is correct for GHS, USD, NGN, GBP, EUR, CNY (the currencies in schema.prisma), but would silently corrupt KWD/BHD/JOD (3 dp) or JPY/KRW (0 dp) if those currencies are added. The hardcoded `* 100` is a magic number with no comment explaining the assumption.
issues.fix: Add a per-currency exponent table (ISO 4217) and compute `amountMinor = Math.round(amount * 10**exponent)`. Reject currencies not in the table at the schema validation layer (z.enum). Document the assumption with a unit test that covers 0/2/3 decimal-place currencies.

issues.title: Idempotency records are only opportunistically expired — stale replays survive
issues.description: checkIdempotency deletes expired records with `deleteMany({where:{expiresAt:{lt:new Date()}}}).catch(()=>{})` on every read — but only the records that match the WHERE clause. A record that expired but isn't returned by the deleteMany (e.g. the delete failed silently) will still match the findUnique on line 199 because the findUnique doesn't filter by expiresAt. So an expired idempotency record can still replay a cached response, returning a 200 for a request that should now be re-processed. The catch() also swallows delete errors.
issues.fix: Add `expiresAt: { gt: new Date() }` to the findUnique where clause so expired records are treated as not-found. Remove the `.catch(()=>{})` on the deleteMany — let it throw so we know about DB issues. Run a scheduled job (BullMQ repeatable or Temporal workflow) to delete expired records every hour instead of doing it inline on every read.

architecture_recommendation.orchestration: Temporal (self-hosted Temporal Server cluster, or Temporal Cloud during the first 12 months to avoid ops burden). Go SDK for workflow + activity implementations. Workflows: PaymentWorkflow, PayoutWorkflow, PayrollRunWorkflow, WebhookDeliveryWorkflow, KycVerificationWorkflow, RefundWorkflow.
architecture_recommendation.database: PostgreSQL 16 (primary OLTP). Prisma stays for the Next.js BFF; the Go service uses pgx + sqlc for hand-tuned SQL. Schema lives in one place (sqlc migrations or Prisma migrate), both services share it. Add: row-level locks for idempotency (pg_advisory_xact_lock), JSONB for metadata/payload columns, partial unique indexes for soft-deleted rows, logical replication to a read replica for analytics.
architecture_recommendation.queue: Redis 7 (already in docker-compose) for: (a) rate limiting via @upstash/ratelimit or ioredis Lua, (b) BullMQ for short-lived fire-and-forget jobs (email, SMS, audit-log fanout, KYC async), (c) Temporal's persistence backend (Temporal supports Postgres or MySQL as its own DB — use a separate `temporal` database on the same Postgres cluster, or Cassandra at scale). Long-running durable workflows (payment, payout, payroll, webhook delivery with backoff) go through Temporal, NOT BullMQ.
architecture_recommendation.rationale: Golang + Temporal is the right choice for Nexora's payment-orchestration core. The current architecture's three existential problems — non-durable execution, no saga/compensation, and a TOCTOU idempotency race — are exactly what Temporal was built to solve. A Payment is naturally a Temporal workflow: Authorise → Capture → Settle → Notify, with each step an idempotent Activity that retries with backoff and compensates on failure (RefundWorkflow). Go's goroutines, ~10ms cold start, and strong gRPC/HTTP story are ideal for the gateway tier that fronts TheTeller/Paystack/Flutterwave. Rust+Tokio is overkill (Nexora's bottleneck is gateway round-trips, not CPU); Elixir+Phoenix is excellent but has a smaller West-African talent pool and no Temporal-quality workflow engine; Node+BullMQ is fine for fire-and-forget jobs but is not a workflow engine — by the time you hand-roll saga/compensation/replay you've reinvented a worse Temporal; Java+Spring Cloud is enterprise-grade but heavyweight and slow to iterate for a startup. Keep Next.js/TS for the marketing site, docs, dashboard, and a thin BFF that calls the Go service via gRPC or REST — this preserves the team's TS skill set and lets you hire 1–2 senior Go engineers for the core.
architecture_recommendation.migration_plan:
Strangler-fig in 6 phases over ~6 months, zero-downtime throughout.

Phase 0 (week 1–2): Stand up infrastructure — Postgres (replace SQLite), Redis, Temporal Server (Temporal Cloud initially), Sentry, structured logging (pino), and OpenTelemetry. Switch DATABASE_URL to Postgres, run prisma migrate, verify all routes work against Postgres. Fix the idempotency race (issue #1) by adding `expiresAt` filter + Postgres advisory locks. Fix the sandbox-key and master-key issues (issues #6, #7).

Phase 1 (week 3–6): Extract the webhook dispatcher to a Temporal WebhookDeliveryWorkflow. dispatchWebhook() becomes `workflowClient.ExecuteWorkflow(DeliverWebhookWorkflow, ...)` and returns immediately. The workflow does the HTTP POST + backoff via workflow.Sleep() and is replay-safe. Next.js routes call the workflow via a thin Go gRPC gateway (or directly via the Temporal Go SDK if you keep it in Node with temporalio-node-sdk — recommended for the first phase to avoid the Go rewrite).

Phase 2 (month 2–3): Build the Go orchestration service for the core payment flow. PaymentWorkflow: ValidateInput → CreatePaymentRow (Postgres tx) → InitiateTheTeller (Activity, retryable) → WaitForCallback (workflow.Signal or workflow.ExecuteActivity polling) → VerifyTransaction (Activity) → UpdatePaymentRow → DispatchWebhook (child workflow). Next.js POST /v1/payments becomes a thin proxy: validate body, call `workflowClient.StartWorkflow(PaymentWorkflow, ...)`, return the workflow_id as the payment id. GET /v1/payments/[id] queries Postgres directly (or polls workflow status).

Phase 3 (month 3–4): Migrate PayoutWorkflow and PayrollRunWorkflow to Go+Temporal. PayrollRunWorkflow fans out to per-employee PayoutWorkflows as child workflows — Temporal handles the saga: if 49 of 50 succeed and the 50th fails, you can compensate the 49 or retry the 50th without losing state. Add the background worker that was missing (issue #8) — Temporal workers ARE the background worker.

Phase 4 (month 4–5): Add the missing CRUD endpoints (issues #10–#14) — refunds, payment-links, DELETE on virtual-cards/foreign-accounts/webhook-endpoints, PATCH/execute on payroll runs. Each new state-changing endpoint starts a Temporal workflow.

Phase 5 (month 5–6): Implement real KYC vendor integration (issue #15) as a Temporal KycVerificationWorkflow with human-in-the-loop (Temporal Signals) for manual review when sanctions/PEP screening flags a match. Add the missing 405 Allow headers (issue #20), structured logging (issue #21), and request body size limits (issue #17). Cut over the rate limiter to Redis (issue #4). Decommission any remaining inline backoff code.

Throughout: every Temporal workflow is versioned using Temporal's Patch + Versioning APIs so in-flight workflows continue on the old version while new starts use the new version — this is the zero-downtime guarantee. The Next.js routes proxy to the Go service throughout, so the public API contract never changes. Deploy with blue/green on the Go service; Temporal workers drain in-flight workflows on shutdown via worker.Stop().

Validate: replay-safety (kill worker mid-workflow, restart, verify it resumes), retry behavior (mock 503 from TheTeller, verify backoff), compensation (mock failure at Verify step, verify payment marked failed + webhook dispatched).
